extracted.intended_audience: public relations practitioners, political leaders, educators, university and civic organizers (including women's organizations)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance and standards for planning and executing propaganda or public-relations campaigns across politics, education, civic organizations, and higher education institutions. Emphasizes creation of circumstances, timing, use of prominent endorsers, publicity offices, and training in technique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leader must create circumstances, not merely reflect them
rubrics_metrics.description: The political leader must be a creator of circumstances, not only a creature of mechanical processes of stereotyping and rubber stamping.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rather than simply arguing issues (e.g., telling voters 'high tariff increases costs'), construct events and settings that dramatize and make the contention self-evident (examples: staged exhibitions in many cities, ceremonious inaugurations by prominent people, organized agitations by affected groups). This pre-keys public attention so direct appeals answer spontaneous questions and emotional demands.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use modern mechanisms as instruments within a planned strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: He may use the modern mechanism of the radio ... but he will almost certainly use the psychological method of approach which was old in Andrew Jackson's day. If he were a propagandist, he would still use the radio, but as one instrument of a well-planned strategy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine mass media channels (radio/newspapers) with staged events, exhibitions, and ceremonies. Media alone is insufficient; integrate communication channels into a broader campaign of circumstances creation and dramatization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Create dramatic, demonstrable evidence for claims
rubrics_metrics.description: He not merely would tell people that the high tariff increases the cost of the things they buy, but would create circumstances which would make his contention dramatic and self-evident.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: simultaneous exhibitions in many cities showing added costs due to tariff, tagging merchandise with comparative prices, boycotts of certain goods, soliciting expert (e.g., social worker) testimony to dramatize social effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stage events with prominent, independent endorsers
rubrics_metrics.description: He would see that these exhibitions were ceremoniously inaugurated by prominent men and women who were interested in a low tariff apart from any interest in his personal political fortunes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use respected third-party figures to inaugurate or endorse events so the message appears broader than the candidate's self-interest; helps create credibility and wider acceptance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precondition public attention before direct appeals
rubrics_metrics.description: In whatever ways he dramatized the issue, the attention of the public would be attracted to the question before he addressed them personally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure public awareness and emotional readiness through prior events and dramatization so that subsequent speeches or broadcasts resonate rather than feel like an intrusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider global news rhythms and timing
rubrics_metrics.description: The importance of taking the entire world public into consideration before planning an important event is shown by the wise action of Thomas Masaryk ... Czecho-Slovakia officially became a free state on Monday ... because the press would have more space to devote to it on Monday morning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose dates/times to maximize press coverage and receptivity (e.g., avoid weekends for major announcements). Use cable and news cycle dynamics to 'make history for the cables.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Truthful or social propaganda endures; dishonest propaganda self-defeats
rubrics_metrics.description: The only propaganda which will ever tend to weaken itself as the world becomes more sophisticated and intelligent, is propaganda that is untrue or unsocial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure messages are not fundamentally dishonest or antisocial; as public sophistication grows, false propaganda loses effectiveness and will tend to defeat itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propaganda requires fertile ground — leader must have something public wants
rubrics_metrics.description: There has to be fertile ground for the leader and the idea to fall on. But the leader also has to have some vital seed to sow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Propaganda cannot manufacture desire out of nothing; ensure the message resonates with existing public needs or sentiments, otherwise efforts will fail despite good technique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish propaganda leadership from trial-balloon politics
rubrics_metrics.description: A political practice ... is the technique of the trial balloon ... The politician sends up his balloon ... waits for reverberations ... On the basis of these repercussions he then publicly adopts, rejects or modifies policy. It is a method which has little justification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rather than testing and reacting clumsily, a skilled propagandist should aim to lead public opinion by planning and shaping circumstances; avoid over-reliance on trial balloons as they imply following rather than leading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propagandist's approach: set objectives, know the public, modify circumstances
rubrics_metrics.description: The whole basis of successful propaganda is to have an objective and then to endeavor to arrive at it through an exact knowledge of the public and modifying circumstances to manipulate and sway that public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Begin with a clear objective, conduct accurate audience analysis, and deliberately shape the environment (events, endorsements, media cues) to achieve the objective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leaders should be trained in propaganda technique as well as ideals
rubrics_metrics.description: The political leader of to-day should be a leader as finely versed in the technique of propaganda as in political economy and civics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include propaganda/PR technique in leadership training so leaders can proactively shape public opinion rather than merely reflect it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Government should institutionalize public-information expertise
rubrics_metrics.description: There should, I believe, be an Assistant Secretary of State who is familiar with the problem of dispensing information to the press ... The United States Government should create a Secretary of Public Relations as member of the President's Cabinet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create senior public-relations officials who can analyze public thought, advise on disclosure, interpret national aims internationally, and keep citizens informed; distinguish this role from mere press agents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public relations function is broader than press dispensing
rubrics_metrics.description: The function of the propagandist is much broader in scope than that of a mere dispenser of information to the press.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public-relations professionals should analyze trends, create circumstances, dramatize issues, high-spot significant events, and interpret between government and people — not just issue releases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use propaganda as 'enlightened expert education' via dramatization
rubrics_metrics.description: Call it, if you prefer, government by education. But education, in the academic sense of the word, is not sufficient. It must be enlightened expert propaganda through the creation of circumstances, through the high-spotting of significant events, and the dramatization of important issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine educational aims with persuasive staging and PR techniques to focus public attention and produce intelligent action from a heterogeneous electorate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Women's organizations should use organized propaganda to influence legislation
rubrics_metrics.description: Women's most obvious influence is exerted when they are organized and armed with the weapon of propaganda. ... These organizations map out a legislative program and then use the modern technique of propaganda to make this legislative program actually pass into the law of the land.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Form coalitions, publish literature (bulletins, election information), hold courses and demonstrations, and mobilize group leadership to advance specific legislative agendas (examples include welfare legislation, eight-hour day for women, Shepard-Towner Bill).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use practical, attention-getting tactics (renting spaces/exhibits) to recruit support
rubrics_metrics.description: Some years ago, the Consumers' Committee of Women ... rented an empty store ... and set up an exhibit of merchandise tagging each item with the current price and the price it would cost if the tariff went through. Hundreds of visitors to this shop rallied to the cause of the committee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create accessible, tangible demonstrations (pop-up exhibits, shops, visual price comparisons) to convert passersby into supporters; these tactics turn abstract policy into immediate experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clubs and civic groups should concentrate on public-good projects and use PR to advance them
rubrics_metrics.description: The woman's club ... stands ready to initiate or help any movement which has for its object a distinct public good in the community. ... it constitutes an organized channel through which women can make themselves felt as a definite part of public opinion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify local public-good projects (health, parks, arts, education), run campaigns (e.g., cooking schools, milk in schools, baby health stations), cooperate with radio and other media, and use organized club networks to mobilize opinion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Educators must act as propagandists to raise public appreciation for education
rubrics_metrics.description: The educator has been trained to stimulate to thought the individual students in his classroom, but has not been trained as an educator at large of the public. ... The teaching profession ... has the right to carry on a very definite propaganda with a view to enlightening the public and asserting its intimate relation to the society which it serves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Train teachers (starting in normal schools) to communicate the social value of education to the wider public, advocate for better pay and status, and run campaigns that improve recruitment and public support for education.

rubrics_metrics.name: Universities must 'sell' themselves to secure public and donor support
rubrics_metrics.description: The state university is therefore in an unfortunate position unless its president happens to be a man of outstanding merit as a propagandist and a dramatizer of educational issues. ... The state university prospers according to the extent to which it can sell itself to the people of the state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain active publicity offices/news bureaus, high-spot public-interest work, educate alumni, and present research discoveries in forms the public can understand to attract legislative or private support — while avoiding over-politicization or transforming the institution into a mere tool of political groups or donors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance public appeal with scholarly integrity; avoid making the institution a political instrument
rubrics_metrics.description: If the university shapes its whole policy toward gaining the support of the state legislature—its educational function may suffer. It may be tempted to base its whole appeal to the public on its public service ... This may generate a number of evils ... making the university a political instrument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public relations should not push institutions to compromise core academic missions; when advising on publicity, consider whether the institution itself needs modification rather than simply greater exposure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use news bureaus and professional publicity with ethical standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Many colleges have already developed intelligent propaganda ... in the form of college news bureaus. ... The Association endeavors to uphold the ethical standards of the profession and aims to work in harmony with the press.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establish official news bureaus, participate in intercollegiate associations, publish newsletters, and uphold ethical norms in interaction with the press to promote understanding and avoid adversarial relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Popularize scholarly discoveries in dramatic, public-friendly forms
rubrics_metrics.description: Many of our leading universities rightly feel that the results of their scholarly researches should not only be presented to libraries and learned publications, but should also, where practicable and useful, be given to the public in the dramatic form which the public can understand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hire publicity personnel to translate technical research into compelling narratives and media-ready stories (example: press coverage of the Harvard professor's Mayan discovery), increasing public appreciation and institutional prestige.

rubrics_metrics.name: If public impression is incorrect, either modify the impression or the institution
rubrics_metrics.description: If his institution does not produce the mental picture which it should, one of two things may be wrong: Either the media of communication with the public may be wrong or unbalanced; or his institution may be at fault.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public-relations counsel should diagnose whether a communications problem (wrong media/messaging) or a substantive institutional problem is causing an unfavorable public image and recommend either altering communications or changing institutional practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design public-facing programs (extension courses) with PR-aware planning
rubrics_metrics.description: Many colleges maintain extension courses ... But, to take another example, if they have been badly planned, from the point of view of public relations, if they are unduly scholastic and detached, their effect may be the opposite of favorable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before promoting outreach programs, ensure their content and format match public expectations; if programs are poorly designed, improve them rather than only increasing publicity.

rubrics_metrics.name: High-spot undergraduate or publicly relevant work to correct misperceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: If there is the general opinion that the work of a certain institution is 80 per cent postgraduate research ... If it is false, it should be corrected by high-spotting undergraduate activities. If true, the most should be made of that fact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use publicity to emphasize aspects of institutional work that align with desired public perception; either highlight undergraduate activities or publicize research breakthroughs depending on reality and PR goals.
